name: How Radiology Opened New Doors for Zahra Rahmatullah

content.title: How Radiology Opened New Doors for Zahra Rahmatullah
content.summary: At AKU, Zahra discovered her potential to lead, innovate, and inspire others

media.alt: How Radiology Opened New Doors for Zahra Rahmatullah

content.text: "I always knew I wanted to go into medicine," says AKU alumna Zahra Rahmatullah. "There was nothing else that appealed to me." Growing up near AKU's Stadium Road campus in Karachi, she often looked up at the red-brick hospital building and told her family, "I want to study there."

Years later, that childhood dream came true. As a medical student at AKU, Zahra found herself drawn to every discipline she encountered - which made choosing one difficult. Eventually, her curiosity led her to radiology. "Every single surgeon, every pulmonologist-whatever rotation you're in-will call up radiology and ask, 'Hey, the scan of my patient-what do you think?'" she says. "It's underrated but absolutely essential, and it allows you to access every aspect of medicine."

Radiology also started her on a journey that would eventually lead her to the stage of the annual meeting of Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), the world's largest radiology conference. "It was one of those moments where you think, 'If I've done this, I can do anything,'" she reflected.

It all began with the mentorship of residents and faculty who, as she puts it, "taught me from scratch." Together, they used a large dataset to study abdominal-pelvic injuries in bomb blast victims - a grim but vital subject in Pakistan's context. "In resource-limited countries, you don't have the capacity to scan patients multiple times; you don't have the time or the resources," she explains. "Our findings can help first responders and doctors treat patients faster and more effectively. That's the goal."

The study was one of a handful selected from tens of thousands for an oral presentation at RSNA. "It was surreal," Zahra says. "I was on a panel with professors from Harvard and China - and there I was, a medical student from Karachi."

Beyond research, Zahra's years at AKU also cultivated her approach and leadership. Through Falah, AKU's student-run social welfare organization, she learned to hold onto compassion, even on the most gruelling days. "You treat patients differently when you know they've sold everything they had to come for care," she says.

As Vice President of the Student Research Forum, she helped organize AKU's first student-led research conference, bringing together students from across Pakistan and other AKU campuses. It was a monumental task, but for Zahra, it was deeply personal. "Research is very important simply because it's the future," she reflects. "We have so many students in Pakistan with great ideas but just not a forum to express them. I wanted to help create a space where other students could really see what they're capable of."

Her training gave her the confidence to later thrive at Johns Hopkins University, where she stood "shoulder to shoulder with students from some of the world's best institutions," she says. Zahra graduated with a Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) in 2024.
"Being at AKU allowed me to dive headfirst into experiences that tested me and showed me what I was capable of," Zahra reflects. "And in empowering me, AKU has helped me empower others."
